title: Weekend On-Call
narrative:
You're on weekend on-call. It's Saturday afternoon. You're at a BBQ. Your phone buzzes.

"A user can't log in." Minor issue. Probably nothing.

You ignore it. 20 minutes later, the monitoring dashboard lights up red. It's not just one user. It's ALL users.

Your BBQ is about to become a war room.

success.text: You remote in during the BBQ. It was a bad deploy. You fix it in 15 minutes. Everyone at the BBQ is impressed by your dedication (and slightly concerned).
success.log: Solved login crisis from a BBQ.

failure.text: You're distracted by the BBQ. It takes 2 hours to notice and fix. The VP of Sales was one of the affected users.

success.text: The team lead jumps in while you're at the BBQ. They fix it. You're not blamed because you followed protocol.

failure.text: The team lead is also at a BBQ. Nobody answers. The issue persists for 3 hours.

choices.text: Find the root cause, not just the patch

success.text: You skip the BBQ, trace the login failure to a certificate that expired at noon, and fix it at the source. When the team lead calls, you're already typing the postmortem. The burgers can wait. They do.
success.log: Found and fixed the root cause over the BBQ.

failure.text: You trace the issue for six hours and find the root cause — a config change made by a contractor in 2023. You fix it, but the postmortem has a section titled "why this took so long," and it's all about you.
failure.log: Found the root cause. Six hours too late.

title: Mentor a Junior Developer
narrative:
A new junior dev has joined the team. They're enthusiastic but... they wrote a function that queries the entire database on every page load.

They ask you for a code review. The PR is 800 lines of... questionable decisions.

Your manager says: "You'll mentor them this quarter."

choices.text: Sit with them and teach through the problems

success.text: You pair program with them. They learn and improve. Two weeks later, they're shipping solid code. You've made a great colleague.

failure.text: They don't quite get it. You end up rewriting their code yourself. It takes 3x longer than if you'd just done it.

success.text: They're self-motivated and learn from the docs. They come to you with smart questions. Good mentorship!

failure.text: They read the docs but still don't understand. You get frustrated. They feel discouraged.

success.text: You pair on the 800-line PR, find the N+1 query on line 47, and make them fix it themselves while you watch. "Oh," they say, quietly, like they've seen a ghost. Next week their PR is 200 lines.
success.log: Found the N+1 query together. They got it.

failure.text: You pair for three hours and fix the query, but the real problem is that they don't understand the data model. You've bought them three more weeks of 800-line PRs.
failure.log: Fixed the symptom, not the gap.

title: Performance Crisis
narrative:
The app is slow. Really slow. Average page load: 8 seconds. Users are complaining. Churn is up 15%.

Your task: "Make it fast." No specifics on how. The CEO wants it "fixed by next sprint."

You open the profiler. The app makes 47 API calls per page load. Forty. Seven.

success.text: You add Redis caching and reduce API calls from 47 to 3. Page load drops to 800ms. The CEO is thrilled. "This is why we pay you!"

failure.text: You cache aggressively but introduce stale data bugs. Users see old information. Now you have TWO problems.

choices.text: Rewrite the frontend — it's the bottleneck

success.text: You identify the rendering bottleneck and optimize it. You use virtualization and code splitting. Performance improves 5x.

failure.text: The bottleneck wasn't the frontend — it was the backend. You've optimized nothing. The CEO is not happy.

success.text: You present a realistic 3-phase plan. Leadership appreciates the honesty. You get 2 months instead of 2 weeks. Better outcome overall.

failure.text: Leadership doesn't understand. "Just make it fast" they say. You're back to square one with less time.

title: Demo Day
narrative:
It's demo day. You've been building this feature for 3 weeks. The executives are watching via video call.

Your code works on your machine. The staging environment is... questionable. The production environment is a mystery.

You hit "play."

success.text: Staging works perfectly. The demo is smooth. The executives are impressed. "This is why we invest in infrastructure!"

failure.text: Staging is broken. You fumble through it. The demo shows a 404 error. The VP of Marketing laughs nervously.

choices.text: Demo the cool parts, skip the broken parts

success.text: You're a smooth operator. The demo focuses on what works. The broken parts are "known issues in beta." Everyone is impressed.
success.log: Smooth demo — they didn't notice the broken parts.

failure.text: An executive asks to see the feature you skipped. "Can you show me the search?" You have no search. It's on fire.
failure.log: Executive asked for the broken feature. 💀

success.text: Against all odds, everything works. The demo is flawless. You're a hero. The universe has blessed your deployment.

failure.text: The gods are not pleased. The demo crashes. The video call freezes. The audio cuts out. It's a triple crown of failures.

title: The Code Review from Hell
narrative:
Your PR has been sitting for 5 days. The senior dev finally comments: "Can you explain your thinking here? And here? And here? Also, have you considered rewriting this in Rust? And why are you using JavaScript in 2024?"

There are 47 comments. 3 of them are questions. 44 of them are "nitpicks."

success.text: You respond professionally and explain your tradeoffs. The senior dev says "Fair point." PR approved. You've earned respect.

failure.text: You get defensive. The conversation turns personal. The PR sits for another week.

success.text: You make the changes. It's tedious but you learn something. PR approved after 2 more rounds.

failure.text: You make the changes but introduce new bugs. The review cycle never ends. You've been in this PR for 3 weeks.

success.text: You ask the senior dev to prioritize: "What are the 3 most important changes?" They respond with a focused list. PR gets approved.

failure.text: They say "everything needs work." It's not helpful. You're stuck.

title: The AI Vibe Code
narrative:
You've been assigned a complex feature with a tight deadline. You try AI code generation — it produces 200 lines of code that looks perfect.

You run the tests. They all pass. You deploy it. The feature works.

Two days later, the monitoring dashboard shows a memory leak. The AI-generated code is consuming 500MB of RAM per request. Nobody knows why.

You wrote none of this code. You don't understand how it works.

choices.text: Read the AI-generated code line by line to find the leak

success.text: You spend 4 hours reading the generated code. You find it — an unclosed database connection in a loop. You fix it and add a comment explaining why.
success.log: Found the leak through careful reading!

failure.text: The code is 200 lines of AI-generated spaghetti. You can't follow the logic. You're stuck.

choices.text: Rewrite the feature from scratch without AI

success.text: You rewrite it yourself. It's 50 lines of clean, readable code. No memory leak. The team is impressed.
success.log: Wrote it clean — no AI needed!

failure.text: You rewrite it but miss some edge cases. The feature works but crashes on invalid input.

choices.text: Add a memory limit and alert — treat it as a symptom, not the cause

success.text: You add a memory limit and alert. The leak is contained. You buy time to investigate properly.

failure.text: The memory limit triggers too late. The service crashes before the alert fires.

choices.text: Ask the AI tool for an explanation of the generated code

success.text: Miraculously, the AI tool explains its own code. You find the leak in 10 minutes. You feel like you've hacked reality.

failure.text: The AI tool gives you a vague explanation that doesn't help. You're back to square one.

title: The AI Code Review
narrative:
You've integrated an AI code reviewer into your workflow. It catches typos, suggests improvements, and flags potential bugs.

Today it flags 47 issues in your PR. Most are minor — naming suggestions, style complaints. But one says: "Potential security vulnerability: SQL injection in user input."

You didn't write any SQL. You don't even use a database in this feature.

choices.text: Investigate the SQL injection claim thoroughly

success.text: You trace the code and find it — a third-party library you're using constructs a query unsafely. You replace it with a parameterized version.

failure.text: You investigate but can't find the issue. The AI was wrong. You approve the PR and move on.
failure.log: AI was wrong. Nothing to fix.

choices.text: Dismiss it as a false positive — AI reviewers are noisy

success.text: You dismiss it. The PR passes. Two weeks later, a hacker exploits the exact vulnerability the AI flagged. You feel terrible.
success.log: AI was right. You were wrong. 💀

failure.text: You dismiss it. It was a false positive. The PR passes. You feel smug.
failure.log: AI was wrong. You were right.

choices.text: Ask a senior dev to review the AI's claim

success.text: The senior dev agrees it's a real issue. You fix it together. They say "good catch — AI reviewers can be helpful when you take them seriously."

failure.text: The senior dev says "ignore the AI. It's noisy." You approve the PR.

title: The AI Library Dependency
narrative:
You've been using an AI-generated library for data processing. It's fast, well-documented, and works perfectly.

Today you see a GitHub issue: "Critical vulnerability in v2.3.1 — arbitrary code execution via crafted input."

Your code uses v2.3.1. You didn't write the vulnerable code. You just imported the library.

success.text: You upgrade. The new version works perfectly. You add a note to the team about dependency hygiene.

failure.text: The new version has breaking changes. Your code breaks in 3 places. You fix them but it takes all day.

choices.text: Audit your usage of the library to see if the vulnerability applies

success.text: You audit your code and find you're using the library safely. The vulnerability requires a specific input pattern you don't use. You sleep easy.

failure.text: You can't determine if you're vulnerable. The library is complex. You upgrade anyway.

choices.text: Replace the library with a custom implementation

success.text: You write your own data processing code. It's slower but you control it. No more dependency risk.

failure.text: Your implementation is buggy. It processes data incorrectly. You revert and upgrade instead.

choices.text: Ignore it — the vulnerability is theoretical

success.text: You ignore it. Nothing happens. The vulnerability is theoretical. You feel lucky.

failure.text: A hacker exploits the vulnerability. Your data is compromised. The incident takes 3 days to resolve.

title: The AI Prompt Disaster
narrative:
You need to write a complex regex for log parsing. You try AI — it gives you a regex that works on your test data.

You deploy it to production. It works on 99% of logs. But the 1% it misses causes silent data corruption.

The corrupted logs are indistinguishable from valid ones. You don't notice for a week.

choices.text: Write the regex yourself from scratch

success.text: You write a robust regex that handles all edge cases. It's longer than the AI version but correct.

failure.text: You write a regex but miss an edge case. It's better than the AI version but still broken.

choices.text: Add validation checks for the corrupted logs

success.text: You add validation that catches the corrupted logs. You fix them and add a monitoring alert for future issues.

failure.text: Your validation is too strict — it catches valid logs too. You block legitimate data.

choices.text: Ask the AI to improve the regex with more test cases

success.text: You feed the AI the corrupted logs as test cases. It generates a better regex that handles the edge cases.
success.log: AI improved with better test cases!

failure.text: The AI generates a more complex regex that's harder to read but still broken. You're worse off.

choices.text: Switch to a different parsing approach — stop using regex

success.text: You switch to a structured parser. It's more reliable and easier to maintain. The team loves it.

failure.text: The structured parser is slower. It can't handle the volume of logs. You revert.

title: The Boss Wants Your Weekend
narrative:
Friday at 4 PM. Your boss walks by: "Hey, we have a deadline Monday morning. Can everyone work this weekend? Just a few hours each day."

You have plans. You have a life. You have a weekend.

Your team is looking at you. You're the senior one now.

success.text: You power through. The deadline is met. Your boss is grateful. But you're exhausted on Monday.

failure.text: You work but you're too tired to be effective. You make a mistake that costs more time than the weekend work saved.

success.text: You propose a realistic plan: work Saturday morning, ship Monday afternoon. The boss agrees. Work-life balance preserved.

failure.text: The boss insists. "Everyone else is doing it." You're now known as "the one who wouldn't work weekends."

success.text: You organize a fair rotation. Each person works one day. The work gets done and nobody burns out. You're a natural leader.

failure.text: The rotation falls apart. People don't coordinate. You end up doing the most work. Leadership is happy but you're not.
failure.log: Rotation failed. You did most of the work.

title: The Midnight Hotfix
narrative:
It's 11 PM on a Friday. Your phone buzzes.

"URGENT: Production is down. Need someone to push a hotfix ASAP."

You're at dinner with friends. Your phone has 47 unread messages from the on-call team.

The hotfix involves changing a single line in a file you've never seen before.

success.text: You find the bug, fix it, and deploy in 20 minutes. Your friends think you're a superhero.

failure.text: You fix the wrong line. Production stays down. Your friends leave without you.

success.text: The senior dev fixes it in 10 minutes. You learn what happened. You're on call next week.
success.log: Handed off to senior. Learned something.

failure.text: The senior dev is asleep. You wait 30 minutes. Production stays down.
failure.log: Senior dev was asleep. Too late.

success.text: You remote in, read the module, and realize the one-line fix is a trap. You rewrite the 40-line function cleanly, add the missing test, and ship it. Production recovers in 40 minutes. The on-call channel goes quiet, which is the best sound in the world.
success.log: Rewrote the module. Production back in 40 minutes.

failure.text: You rewrite the module at 1 AM with the focus of a poet. It ships. It works. It also changes a field name that another service depends on, and now two teams are down instead of one.
failure.log: The rewrite fixed it and broke a neighbor.

title: Technical Debt Avalanche
narrative:
You've been assigned to a new feature. The code you need to modify hasn't been touched in 3 years.

It's written in a framework that's no longer maintained. The comments say "TODO: rewrite this" in 47 places.

The deadline is next week.

success.text: You write a thin wrapper around the legacy code. It's ugly but it works. Feature ships on time.
success.log: Wrapped the legacy mess. Ship it.

failure.text: Your wrapper breaks the whole system. You've made things worse.

success.text: You refactor the legacy code, write tests, and add the feature. It takes 3 weeks but the code is beautiful now.

failure.text: You refactor but miss edge cases. The feature doesn't work. Your manager is not happy.

success.text: You spend three days replacing the 3-year-old module with something you can actually read. The feature lands on time, and for the first time in years someone can say "I understand this code" without sarcasm.
success.log: Replaced the dead module. The feature landed on time.

failure.text: You refactor for a week. The feature is now three days from the deadline, and the rewrite introduced a subtle bug that only appears in production. You've traded 47 TODOs for one incident.
failure.log: The rewrite ate the deadline and shipped a bug.

title: The Mentor Crisis
narrative:
You're mentoring a junior dev who keeps making the same mistake. Over and over.

They fix it. You review it. They break it again the next day.

Your patience is wearing thin. They look defeated.

Their performance review is next week.

choices.text: Sit with them and figure out the root cause

success.text: You discover they don't understand the fundamentals. You create a learning plan. They improve dramatically.
success.log: Found the root cause. They improved!

failure.text: You can't figure out what's wrong. They fail their review. You feel responsible.

choices.text: Tell them to read the documentation

success.text: They read the docs. It clicks. They improve. You're a hands-off mentor.

failure.text: They read the docs but still don't understand. They're frustrated. You're frustrated.

choices.text: Trace the bug to the real problem

success.text: You sit down with their broken PR and trace it: the bug isn't a coding mistake, it's a misunderstanding of how the auth middleware works. You walk through the actual request flow once. They never make the mistake again. The performance review writes itself.
success.log: Found the real gap: the auth middleware.

failure.text: You trace the bug and find the real problem — but explaining it requires a two-hour deep dive they're not ready for. They nod, say "got it," and break it again on Monday.
failure.log: Found it. They weren't ready for it.

title: The 404 That Wasn't
narrative:
A user reports a 404 error. You check the logs. The page exists. The route exists. The code exists.

You check the CDN. You check the load balancer. You check the DNS.

Everything looks fine. But the user still gets a 404.

You've been debugging this for 4 hours. It's 2 AM.

success.text: The user's ISP is blocking the domain. You tell them to use a different network. Problem solved.

failure.text: You spend 2 more hours on the user's network. It's not that. You're exhausted.

success.text: You restart the CDN. The 404 goes away. It was a cache issue. You're a wizard.

failure.text: You restart the CDN. The 404 gets worse. More users are affected.

choices.text: Log it and move on — it's a false alarm

success.text: It was a false alarm. You saved time by not investigating. The team appreciates your pragmatism.

failure.text: It wasn't a false alarm. It was a real issue that you ignored. The problem gets worse.

title: The Refactor Temptation
narrative:
You're assigned to a feature. The code you need to touch is... terrible.

It's a 2,000-line function. It has nested if-statements 12 levels deep. The variable names are single letters.

You know you should refactor first. Your manager says "just ship the feature."

But you can't help yourself. The code is hurting you.

success.text: You refactor the function into clean, testable pieces. Then you add the feature in 2 days.

failure.text: You refactor but introduce bugs. The feature doesn't work. Your manager is not happy.

success.text: You hack together the feature. It works. You add a TODO comment for future refactoring.

failure.text: You hack it together but miss edge cases. The feature breaks in production.

choices.text: Refactor it yourself, module by module

success.text: You split the 2,000-line function into twelve small ones, one commit at a time, with tests after each. It takes a week. The feature lands in week two. Future you sends a thank-you card (metaphorically; future you is just less angry).
success.log: Refactored module by module. The feature shipped.

failure.text: You're on function eight of twelve when the manager's deadline hits. The code is now half-refactored, which is somehow worse than fully terrible, and the feature ships with the refactor still open.

title: The Tech Stack War
narrative:
Your team is divided. Half wants to use Framework X. Half wants Framework Y.

Both sides are passionate. Both sides are right. Both sides are wrong.

The argument has been going on for 3 months. No progress is being made.

You're asked to break the tie.

choices.text: Run a proof of concept for each

success.text: You build a POC with each framework. The data speaks for itself. The team agrees.

failure.text: Both POCs are equal. The team is more divided than ever.

success.text: You flip a coin. Heads wins. Everyone laughs. The team moves on.
success.log: Coin flip settled it. Team moved on.

failure.text: The team is offended by the coin flip. They want a real decision.

choices.text: Benchmark both with a real prototype

success.text: You build the same endpoint in both frameworks, run it through a replay of production traffic, and post the numbers. Framework X is 2.3x faster but 4x the memory. The argument ends. The silence in the channel is beautiful.
success.log: Ended the stack war with real numbers.

failure.text: You build both prototypes, but your benchmark harness has a bug — you forgot to warm the caches. Framework Y "wins" by 3x, and the team ships it. Six months later, everyone remembers your name in the postmortem.
failure.log: The benchmark had a bug. The wrong framework won.

title: The Agile Transformation
narrative:
The CEO just hired an "Agile Transformation Consultant." They cost $250,000.

Tomorrow, your team is going through "Agile." You've never heard of it. Your team lead says it's "just Scrum but more."

You're told to attend a 4-hour "Agile Workshop" on a Friday. Your feature deadline is Monday.

The consultant says: "We're going to break out of our comfort zones!"

success.text: You survive the workshops. You learn that "Agile" mostly means more meetings. But you're now "Agile Certified."

failure.text: The workshops are 8 hours each day. You miss your deadline. Your team hates you.

success.text: You sneak away to code. Nobody notices. You ship your feature on time. The consultant is fooled.
success.log: Code while others did team building.

failure.text: The consultant notices. You're called out in front of the team. Your manager is not happy.

choices.text: Keep your head down and ship the feature

success.text: While the workshop produces 40 sticky notes and a vision board, you ship the feature on Monday. The consultant calls your approach "resistance to change." The PM calls it "great." You take the PM's word.

failure.text: You ship the feature, but the "Agile" process now requires a retro you missed, a story point audit, and a "re-estimation." Your feature is done. Your paperwork isn't.

title: The Sprint Ceremony
narrative:
Your team is doing "Sprint Planning." The PM has 80 story points for a 2-week sprint. Your team's velocity is 30.

The Scrum Master says: "We can do it if we believe!"

Your team lead says: "Just say yes. We'll figure it out."

You know you'll be working weekends.

success.text: You present velocity data. The PM reduces the scope. The sprint is realistic. Your team survives.
success.log: Data saved the team from burnout!

failure.text: The PM says "we'll figure it out." You're stuck with 80 points. Weekend city.

success.text: You power through. It's brutal but you ship. Your team is exhausted but proud.

failure.text: You can't keep up. The sprint fails. Your velocity drops. The Scrum Master adds more ceremonies.

choices.text: Show the metrics from what you've shipped

success.text: You pull the last four sprints: 80 committed, 31 shipped, 9 hours average overtime. The Scrum Master's "if we believe" fades. The PM quietly re-scopes to 40 points. The team lead gives you a look that means "don't do that again." You will absolutely do that again.
success.log: Showed the real numbers. The scope halved.

failure.text: You present the metrics, but the PM already committed 80 points to the roadmap in the all-hands. Your data is now "aspirational," and the sprint proceeds as planned.
failure.log: The data arrived after the commitment.

title: The Deprecation Notice
narrative:
A critical library your project depends on just announced it's being deprecated in 6 months.

There's no direct replacement. You'll need to find an alternative or build your own.

Your team says: "We'll deal with it later."

You know "later" never comes.

success.text: You create a migration plan and present it to leadership. They approve the time. Migration goes smoothly.

failure.text: Leadership says "we'll deal with it later." You start planning anyway. It takes 3x longer.

choices.text: Wait and deal with it later

success.text: You wait. A better replacement appears. You migrate in 2 weeks. Lucky break.

failure.text: You wait. The library stops working. You scramble to find a replacement. Chaos.

success.text: You spend two weekends building a thin adapter layer over the old library. The deprecation date is now a non-event, and when the team finally gets around to it, the migration is a weekend, not a quarter.
success.log: Built the adapter. The deprecation is neutralized.

failure.text: You build the adapter, but you pick the wrong replacement API — the new library changed its semantics between versions. The adapter works perfectly for a library nobody ships with.
failure.log: The adapter targeted the wrong version.

title: BOSS: The Migration Project
narrative:
Your BOSS. The company is migrating from a monolith to microservices. This is the "big one."

You're leading the migration of the user authentication service. It has 14 dependencies, 3 of which are undocumented. The production database has 2 million records.

Deadline: 4 weeks. Team: You and one other mid-level dev.

The migration looms.

success.text: You use the strangler fig pattern. Bit by bit, you migrate functionality. Zero downtime. The boss is impressed.

failure.text: The incremental approach takes too long. The deadline approaches. You're 60% done with 1 week left.

choices.text: Big bang — cut over in one weekend

success.text: You prepare extensively. The cutover happens Saturday night. By Sunday morning, everything works. It was terrifying but it paid off.

failure.text: Something breaks during cutover. The database migration script has a bug. You spend 18 hours restoring from backup.

success.text: You make a compelling case. Leadership gives you 2 more developers and 2 extra weeks. The migration proceeds smoothly.

failure.text: Leadership says "no budget." You're still migrating with your 1.5-person team. The deadline is immovable.
